targets.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) to the high camp near 7,600 ft on the Inspiration Glacier flat. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. For this specific route: from high camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline seen from camp, below an obvious crack leading up to a U-shaped notch in the crest.
targets.descent_text: Descend via Eldorado's standard East Ridge route back toward the glacier camp.

targets.approach: There is no direct trailhead-to-summit trail. Vehicle access to the Elwha Valley has been closed since a May 2021 washout on Olympic Hot Springs Road; you now walk or bike an extra ~6-7 miles from the Madison Falls parking area (past the washout, then up Whiskey Bend Road) just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead. From Whiskey Bend, follow the Elwha River Trail to Chicago Camp, where it fords the Elwha short of Low Divide, then leave the trail and continue about 3 miles cross-country up into Elwha Basin and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763 ft) to reach the north ridge of Mount Queets. Most parties treat this as a multi-day (4+ day round trip) wilderness objective, commonly combined with the Bailey Range Traverse via Queets Basin to the west. The lower third of the north ridge is mostly 2nd-class scrambling on crumbly rock and heather; where it becomes impassable, drop a few hundred feet to traverse steep, firm scree around 5,300 ft on the east side to bypass a cliff band, then regain the ridge for an easy 2nd-class scramble around its west side before a moderately steep snow slope on the east side leads to the summit. Microspikes and an axe have been used here even in late August.
targets.descent: Reverse the south slopes back into the Elwha Basin.
targets.descent_text: Descend the north ridge, retracing the route over Dodwell-Rixon Pass to the Elwha Basin camp.

wa_east_face.approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Middle Gunsight's east face is a known technical objective once on the ridge; expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.
wa_east_face.descent_text: After summiting, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors. Make one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then a second, loose and dirty one into the moat at the base of the notch. Navigate the crevasse field on Chickamin Glacier to return to base camp.
wa_east_face.name: East Face

wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.approach: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. The path climbs steeply through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before breaking out onto talus. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulder field, staying climber's right to avoid an unnecessary crossing of Eldorado Creek, until the talus eases into the open, beautiful alpine Eldorado Creek Basin (a common first camp at roughly 5,400–5,600 ft, ~3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead). From the basin, climb up onto a rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft, then drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (an alternate/second camp at 6,100–6,400 ft, with reliable running water). From Roush Basin, ascend broken talus and slabs onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the exposed, corniced knife-edge summit ridge (in certain conditions a very thin edge with steep — 40–45°+ — flanks; ice axe and crampons essentially mandatory, and rope/running-belay technique is common for less experienced members), continue down through the gap in the lower East Ridge, then rope up again to cross the Inspiration Glacier and descend the Eldorado Glacier back to Roush Basin, over the intervening ridge into Eldorado Creek Basin, and down the boulder field and timbered climbers' trail to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard route; multiple trip reports and guide-service itineraries describe the descent purely in terms of downclimbing and reversing glacier travel, and note that some parties have even skied the ridge and glaciers in spring conditions rather than roping for rappels. Watch for softening snow bridges and increasing crevasse hazard on the glaciers later in the day (afternoon descents in summer are notably less secure than an early-morning ascent), and for the knife-edge becoming icy/firm late-season, which can make the downclimb more consequential an
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: East Ridge (Inspiration Glacier)

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — a long, somewhat complicated route across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–D
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.descent_text: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead (see the East Ridge route for full detail). This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappels required on the descent itself — one party even skied the knife-edge ridge and glacier on the way down. Rappelling comes up on this route only on the approach/entry into the couloir, not on the summit descent: one party used a 40-meter rappel off the Inspiration Glacier side to drop into the couloir's gully system, anchored on two pitons with some newish tat, and noted a full 60m rope would get a party through everything in one rappel rather than needing to downclimb the remainder — but again, this is describing getting into the route, not descending from the summit. Because the descent is the shared East Ridge walk-off, treat glacier crevasse hazard and knife-edge icing exactly as on tha
wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.name: Northwest Couloir / Eldorado Glacier

wa_eldorado_peak_north_ridge.approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to high camp on the Inspiration Glacier, then cross the Inspiration Glacier around the east end of the East Ridge and traverse the glacier on the mountain's north side at about 8,100 ft to the NW Ice Couloir notch at the base of the North Ridge.
wa_eldorado_peak_north_ridge.descent_text: Return down the same ridge system to the notch and back to camp on the Inspiration Glacier; parties who finish via the East Ridge instead descend that ridge's knife-edge back to camp.
wa_eldorado_peak_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.approach: Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, camp near the base of the East Ridge (about 7,500 ft), then cross the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers to Dorado Needle Col and make a loose fourth-class downclimb into the Marble Creek cirque, traversing to the toe of the arete near 6,000 ft. Typically a 3-day trip (approach day, climb day, exit day); the first roughly 800 ft of climbing is Class 4 before harder 5th-class sections.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.descent_text: From the summit, descend the East Ridge — most parties find this significantly easier and more straightforward than downclimbing the loose West Arete — then return to camp via the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier.
wa_eldorado_peak_west_arete.name: West Arete

wa_gunrunner.approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.
wa_gunrunner.descent_text: The traverse climbs the north faces of the four Gunsight summits and rappels their south sides. From South Peak, a rappel descent leads to the Blue Glacier; the last rappel is free-hanging over a gaping moat onto the glacier, so look for the line that clears it. Check every rappel anchor on the granite thoroughly before trusting it. Parties often finish this descent in darkness. The rappels land on the east side of the range: a party camped below the Blue Glacier walks down to camp, while one based at the Dome-Chickamin col must work south below the peaks, cross the Blizzard-Gunsight col back onto the Chickamin Glacier, and recross the glacier to the col. Allow 3-4 hours, depending on snow and crevasse conditions on the glacier.
wa_gunrunner.name: Gunrunner

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (1,400', end of the drivable Suiattle River Road/FR-26 — the road has been closed to vehicles at a flood washout near milepost 4, roughly 16 miles short of the trailhead; while it stays closed, add that road walk or ride to the hike and check its status first), follow Downey Creek Trail #768. The maintained tread climbs gently along Downey Creek, crossing five tributary creeks (one draining Downey/Pilot Lakes can be a difficult ford in spring high water) and passing informal camps at roughly 1.6, 3, 3.5, and 4 miles before reaching the Bachelor Creek crossing at 6.6 miles/2,400'. Expect old-growth blowdown across the tread in places and a brushy avalanche-chute crossing opposite Green Mountain. At Bachelor Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers'/boot path, which follows the north side of the creek (parties report an improved use-trail here that avoids older brushy sections) up to Bachelor Flats and Bachelor Meadows — the common first-night camp and most parties' Day 1 stop. From Bachelor Meadows continue up steepening open slopes to Cub Pass, then drop about 700' to Cub Lake and cross the meadows beyond
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.descent_text: Reverse the ridge crest from the summit: belay/downclimb the exposed summit ridge back down to a large horn about 50' below the true summit that is thickly slung with rappel webbing (a good on-route confirmation marker). From there, make a double-rope (60m x 2) rappel down the West Face to regain the base of the route's black basaltic dike/dihedral. Scramble down several hundred feet of Class 3 terrain on the dike to the top of the crux dihedral, then make a second, diagonal double-rope (60m x 2) rappel — the last person down should place a directional piece of protection to keep the rope running true — which in one pull reaches the snow finger below. From the snow finger, downclimb or glissade back onto the Chikamin Glacier and reverse the approach (re-climb to the Chikamin-Dome col, cross the Dome Glacier, over Itswoot Pass/Cub Pass, down Bachelor Meadows/Bachelor Creek, and out Downey Creek Trail #768) to the trailhead. All anchors reported on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, and chockstones — with no fixed/bolted stations, consistent with its remote, low-traffic character. Typical parties use two 60m ropes for both rappels; expect the crux dihedral's black rock to
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.name: Standard Route

wa_sw_ridge.approach: The east-side multi-day approach: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan to Stehekin, NPS shuttle to High Bridge, ~9-10 miles on the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail, then an off-trail bushwhack and glacier approach (~5,000 ft gain) to a high camp below the peaks.
wa_sw_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors and make two double-rope rappels: the first to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, the second into the moat at the base of the notch (loose, dirty and cold). With a single 60 m rope expect more rappels. From the glacier, reverse the approach: descend roughly 5,000 ft back to Agnes Creek and hike out 9-10 miles to High Bridge.
wa_sw_ridge.name: Southwest Ridge

adams_avalanche_glacier.approach: From Cold Springs trailhead, traverse via round-the-mountain trail to the southwest side of Mount Adams, approach glacier directly from southwest.
adams_avalanche_glacier.descent_text: From the summit, descend south via the South Spur snowfields (or the snowfield adjacent to the Avalanche/White Salmon glaciers) back toward the Morrison Creek/Cold Springs approach, glissading where conditions allow.
adams_avalanche_glacier.name: Avalanche Glacier

adams_northwest_ridge.approach: Forest Service Road 2329 from Taklakh Lake area (5.7 miles). Killen Creek Trail (#113) to Pacific Crest Trail junction, then High Camp Trail (#10) to meadow camp at 6,900 ft.
adams_northwest_ridge.descent_text: Descend along the North Ridge to the Adams Glacier basin high camp, or in ski-descent conditions the route itself can be down-climbed/skied, threading the same rock-band pinch encountered on the ascent.
adams_northwest_ridge.name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.approach: Start at the Killen Creek Trailhead (~4,600 ft), accessed via Forest Roads 23, 21, and 2329 from the Randle/Trout Lake side (FR-2329 is frequently snow-blocked into early summer — several parties have had to park lower and walk or bushwhack an extra mile-plus of road/forest to reach the actual trailhead). Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 for about 3.1 miles through subalpine forest and wildflower meadows, gaining moderately, to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,100 ft. Cross straight over the PCT onto the High Camp Trail and continue about 1.0 mile further to its end at roughly 6,900 ft, at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine — this is the standard High Camp for the route, with some parties pushing slightly higher to sheltered bivy sites (~7,100 ft) in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine. Total approach is roughly 4 miles and ~2,300–2,500 ft of gain to camp. Killen Creek itself, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable flowing water; above High Camp plan on melting snow/glacier ice. The trail's tread thins out and becomes a moraine/gully scramble above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark, whiteout, or heavy snow cover — take a GPS
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.descent_text: This is a serious, committing route, not a car-to-car day climb for most parties — plan on a night at High Camp before the climb, then descend all the way to the car on summit day. The Adams Glacier line tops out on the upper mountain near the North Ridge/Suksdorf area close to the true summit (12,276 ft) rather than requiring a full crater traverse. Nearly all parties descend via the North Ridge (the North Cleaver, the broad rock-and-snow rib between the Adams and Lava Glaciers), which closes the loop back to High Camp and the Killen Creek trailhead without a car shuttle. The North Ridge is non-technical (class 2–3) but has a reputation among climbers for being steep, rocky, and longer than it looks from above, with loose, exposed sections; parties describe a short mixed downclimb move or two on verglas-covered rock low on the ridge before it eases into a snowfield that can be plunge-stepped or carefully glissaded back toward camp. No fixed rappel anchors exist on this descent and none are typically needed — treat it as sustained exposed scrambling/downclimbing with an ice axe rather than a rappel descent (0 rappels), though it's worth carrying a rope and a few slings/rock gear as
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Adams Glacier

wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.approach: Same trailhead and trail as the Lyman Glacier approach: Killen Creek Trail #113 from the Killen Creek Trailhead, about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest (crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5) to the PCT at ~6,100 ft, then the High Camp Trail #10 another 1.0 mile to High Camp/Adams Glacier Meadows (~6,900 ft). From High Camp, the Lava Glacier Headwall is reached more directly than Lyman: traverse off-trail across the lava fields toward the toe of the Lava Glacier without needing to work around Lava Ridge, reaching the base of the headwall (the triangular ice/snow face bounded by the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other). This is glacial/talus terrain with crevasse hazard on the glacier itself. Sources consistently stress climbing this face early season — late spring to early summer — since it becomes icy and rockfall-prone as the snowpack recedes later in summer.
wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge back toward High Camp, the same non-technical but tedious scree/boulder walk-off used for the Adams Glacier and Lyman Glacier routes on this side of the mountain — long, loose volcanic scree, some narrow/exposed sections, and rockfall risk onto other parties, but no rappelling required on the standard line. From High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. The alternative is to continue over the summit and descend the South Climb route to Cold Springs, which lands you at a different trailhead and requires a shuttle.
wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.name: Lava Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.approach: From the Killen Creek Trailhead (FS Rd 2329, ~3 miles from Takhlakh Lake), follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through open, dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles in you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows (last reliable easy water before the high basin), then the trees thin as the trail climbs rockier terrain to meet the PCT (Trail #2000) at roughly 6,100 ft, about 3.1 miles from the trailhead. Continue straight across the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for about 1.0 mile to High Camp / Adams Glacier Meadows at the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine (~6,900 ft) — a common base camp. From High Camp the route leaves maintained trail: traverse east/southeast, off-trail across lava fields and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, crossing the toe of the Lava Glacier, to reach the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This traverse is glacier/talus travel with real route-finding, especially in low-snow years — a rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on glacier ice. The Lyman Glacier itself splits around a rock outcrop; the north lobe (original route) and south lobe (40° lower half on unbroken neve/ice, upper half broken by crevasses and serac walls) both lead to
wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.descent_text: Standard descent is the North Ridge (also called the North Cleaver) or the adjacent snowfield beside it, dropping back toward High Camp — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. It is the least pleasant part of the trip: long stretches of loose, rotten volcanic scree and boulders, occasional narrow/exposed sections, and a real chance of rockfall onto parties below, so groups should spread out and move quickly through the worst of it. No fixed anchors or rappels are used on the standard line; a short rope-assisted downclimb over an isolated rock band is occasionally used by parties uncomfortable with exposure, but this is improvised, not a bolted or standard rappel. Once back at High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend the South Climb route to the Cold Springs trailhead, which requires a car shuttle or a long road walk back to Killen Creek since it's a different trailhead entirely.
wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.name: Lyman Glacier

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.approach: Start from the Bird Creek Road trailhead (~5,700 ft) on the Yakama Reservation side; route-finding across moraines and glacier fields begins around 6,700 ft, reaching Sunrise Camp at 8,300 ft. The Yakama Nation decides each year whether overnight stays are allowed, so plan a single-day push in day-use-only years.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier past Sunrise Camp and out the way you came in to Bird Creek Meadows. Descending the South Spur instead is possible, but it is not a variation on the same day out - it finishes at the Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead on the mountain's south side, reached by an entirely different road system from the Yakama Nation approach this route starts on, so it only works if you have a vehicle waiting there. A party that walks off south without one has left its car on the far side of the mountain.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Mazama Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes.
wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.descent_text: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. Some parties instead carry over and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs, which requires a long car shuttle. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent.
wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_mount_adams_south_climb.approach: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Rd to the Forest Road 23 junction; bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 junction for South Climb, turn left and follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then follow FR 8040 (steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks — no RVs/trailers) for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead (5,600 ft). The trail follows an old roadbed through the burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadows, crosses Round-the-Mountain Trail #9 and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge to the base of the summit snowfields.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.descent_text: Retrace the ascent line: cross back over the shallow summit crater, down over Piker's Peak, and descend the broad snow slopes of Suksdorf/Crescent Ridge to Lunch Counter, then follow the old roadbed back to the trailhead. Glissading is common on the lower snowfields in firm-but-soft conditions; watch for exposed rock and runout hazards in late season as snow recedes.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.name: South Climb (South Spur)

wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Expect a full day just to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before a summit attempt.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.descent_text: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.name: Wilson Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_chaval_scramble.approach: The hike-in starts where FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) reaches the Arrow Creek switchback (~2,220 ft) — this is the trailhead, not a formal one. A boot/fisherman's path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south (right) bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it's reasonably distinct and has occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned, so expect some searching. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence can be an easy boulder-hop by late summer or a genuine wet ford in early season, so check flow before committing (it's the approach's main creek-ford hazard). Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder and brush (the worst brush of the day) trending southeast, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000–4,300 ft — this is the route-finding crux of the approach: intermittent cairns/flagging at best, and it's easy to end up in the wrong gully. A GPS track of a prior ascent (or careful use of a described waypoint like Point 4593') is genuinely useful here. The last dependable water is
wa_mount_chaval_scramble.descent_text: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing the side creek near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow pat
wa_mount_chaval_scramble.name: West Route

wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley Trailhead (~1,650 ft) at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are deceptively easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail follows the East Fork Foss River through regenerated second-growth forest (logged in the 1930s), entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles. Around the 5-mile mark the trail crosses the East Fork Foss River on a footlog with a handwire (the river runs high and cold under it in early-season snowmelt, so plan the crossing for morning low flow) and then turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 2,400 ft over the next 3 miles on steep, root-laced switchbacks into Necklace Valley proper. This section is the approach's real crux for tired legs and pack weight. The trail eases again as it reaches Jade Lake (~4,600 ft, ~8-9 miles), then Emerald Lake a quarter mile beyond, then Opal Lake, threading through the swampy, lake-studded Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water throughout, but buggy in early/mid-summer. From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends; continue cross-country (an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus) up and southeas
wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.descent_text: This is a walk-off / downclimb descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line the entire way. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ridge scramble back to the top of the glacier remnant, descend the snow/glacier basin back to La Bohn Gap (watch for softened, sun-cupped snow and any residual crevasse slots in early season), then follow the cairned climbers' path back down through the talus and meadow to La Bohn Lakes/Necklace Basin. Most parties treat this as a multi-day trip (roundtrip totals run 22-26 miles with 5,700-9,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss depending on exact line), descending from the summit back to a La Bohn Lakes or Necklace Basin camp the same day and hiking the remaining ~9-10 miles out to the trailhead — back down through Necklace Basin past Opal, Emerald, and Jade Lakes, down the steep rooty 2,400-ft headwall, back across the East Fork Foss River footlog, and out the long, gentle lower trail — on a subsequent day. No technical rope work is required on the standard route; the notable descent hazards are the same river crossing, loose talus, and glacier-remnant travel encountered on the way in, now tackled with tired legs late in the day.
wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.name: Hinman Glacier / Standard

wa_mount_johnson_standard.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). From Upper Royal Basin the maintained trail ends; head cross-country west up h
wa_mount_johnson_standard.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The class 4 terrain near the summit is the crux of the descent as well as the ascent — the rock is loose enough in spots that most reported difficulty on this peak comes from downclimbing it, so face in and test holds on anything above class 3. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own.
wa_mount_johnson_standard.name: Standard Route

wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.approach: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,400 ft). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail, crossing several creeks, toward the Hester Lake basin (roughly 5-6 miles) before leaving the trail to begin the off-trail scramble.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.descent_text: From the summit, reverse the final ridge scramble to the ~5,400 ft col, traverse back across the steep north side of the east ridge, and downclimb the boulder field to the Hester Lake / Little Hester Lake basin. Pick up the Dingford Creek Trail near the lakes and follow it back to the trailhead. Expect brush, including devil's club, below about 4,000 ft when the route is snow-free; allow extra time — one documented trip took over 10 hours car-to-car.
wa_mount_price_hester_lake_route.name: Hester Lake Route

wa_mount_seattle_south.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it is closed to vehicles at Madison Falls by a washout, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach, up from the North Fork Quinault side, follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack
wa_mount_seattle_south.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
wa_mount_seattle_south.name: South Slopes (Standard)
